A verb of sorting, used of distinguishing one thing from a mixture. What it describes is a division of people who had until then been standing together, which is the sentence before any sentence.
From the root of an agreement kept in view and returned to. Framing the question this way makes the exchange a dispute over an existing contract rather than an accusation from nowhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements were oral, formal and public, made before witnesses who carried them in memory for decades. Opening a dispute with the question whether an agreement had been made was a recognised move, and everyone present would expect the terms to be recited next. Being told to stand apart from a gathering was itself a public verdict, delivered before any penalty was named.
studies.didYouKnow: The form of address used here, children of Adam, appears in only five places in the whole Quran. Four of them are in Surah 7, clustered within a few ayat of each other, and this is the fifth and last. The phrase that sounds like a standard way of addressing humanity is in fact reserved for a handful of moments.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The covenant language reframes the choice being offered. It is not put as a choice between serving and not serving, but between two objects of service, one of which has already been described as an open enemy. The greeting does something similar in the other direction. What the Garden finally amounts to is stated as a word spoken by God, so the reward is described as being addressed rather than as contents received.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same address to warn the children of Adam against the one who stripped their parents.
Gives the same single word as the greeting exchanged there, with praise opening and closing it.
Describes the acknowledgement taken at the beginning that this question about a covenant recalls.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing today that you obey without ever having decided to: a notification you answer mid-sentence, a craving you act on before you have registered it, a schedule nobody imposed. Name it out loud once. The passage says service is happening either way, and the first step is finding out what is currently receiving yours.

studies.title: Did You Not Reason
studies.meaning: The address is to people being sorted at the reckoning, and it turns on one accusation. He led astray from among you a great many, and then the question: did you not use your reason. The charge is not that they lacked information but that they did not think. The Fire is then identified as the very thing they had been promised, and the last line names the ground of the outcome. The commentators note that reason is treated throughout as a faculty they possessed and left unused.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, part of a scene at the Judgement that opens by recalling a covenant made with the Children of Adam. The audience had no shortage of intelligence and knew it; Mecca ran on negotiation, poetry, contracts and calculation. No occasion is reported. Putting the charge as a failure of reasoning rather than of information suited a city that could not claim it had never been told anything.

keyTerms.note: A large body of people taken as a mass, from a root about something moulded or formed in quantity. The word occurs only once in the Quran in this form.
From the word for the tether that keeps a camel from wandering. Reason in Arabic is what holds a person in place, which makes losing it a matter of drifting rather than of being stupid.

keyTerms.gloss: enter it and feel its heat
keyTerms.note: A verb for coming close enough to a fire to be scorched by it, used of roasting meat over coals. It names exposure to heat rather than being consumed and finished.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The tether behind the word for reason was literal equipment. A camel left untied wandered off in the night and might be lost or taken, so tying it was the last thing a man did before sleeping, and a well-known saying pairs tying the animal with trusting God. An audience that used one word for a hobbling rope and for the mind heard this as a charge of carelessness.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the great multitude that was led astray occurs only once in the whole Quran. The question that follows it, whether they used their reason, returns six ayat later in this same surah as another question of the same shape, and the Arabic word behind it is the ordinary term for the rope that keeps a camel from wandering off.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is located in a faculty rather than in access to information. That is a hard position and the passage states it plainly: being misled by an enemy is not offered as an excuse, because the capacity to notice was in place. It also implies that the enemy works by suggestion rather than force, since what was lost is something that could have been reasoned through. The Fire is then named simply as what had already been promised.

crossReferences.why: States the same outcome from the other side, that the enemy's assessment of them proved correct.
Records the misleading in the enemy's own words, a promise to lead them and stir false desires in them.
Gives his speech at the reckoning, disclaiming any power beyond calling them and being answered.

studies.applyIt: Take one belief you hold mainly because the people around you hold it. It need not be a religious one. Spend five minutes actually reasoning it through, on paper, as though you had to defend it to somebody fair. The accusation in this ayah is not that they were fooled. It is that the equipment for noticing was sitting there unused.

studies.title: Their Hands Will Speak
studies.meaning: The mouth is sealed and the body gives evidence. Hands speak, feet testify, and what they testify about is what the person earned. The commentators point to the exactness of the arrangement: the organ that could lie is closed, and the organs that carried out the actions are opened. Nothing external is brought in as a witness. The record is the body itself, which leaves no way to dispute the account without disputing your own limbs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the Judgement scene that has just identified the Fire. Testimony in that society was oral and contested, and cases turned on whose word carried more weight and who could produce witnesses to back it. No occasion is reported for the ayah. Evidence that could not be coached or bought answered a real experience of disputes in which a powerful man's word usually settled the matter.

keyTerms.note: The verb for pressing a signet into clay or wax to close something. It implies shutting and marking together, and the same root gives the word for the act that completes a thing.
An intensive form of the verb to speak, and it is addressed to God rather than to a court at large. The hands report to the one asking rather than arguing against their owner.
The verb for acquiring by effort, used of trade. Actions are treated as things a person accumulates rather than as events that happen and pass, which is why they can be produced later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A seal was a working tool. Merchants pressed a signet into clay to close a letter or a jar so that tampering would show, and a man's seal stood for him in his absence. Sealing a mouth would therefore have read as putting something beyond further alteration rather than as mere silencing. And in a world of oral testimony, evidence that nobody could get at was close to unimaginable.
studies.didYouKnow: Three passages of the Quran describe the body testifying, and each names different parts. One gives tongues, hands and feet. Another gives hearing, sight and skins, and adds a short exchange in which the accused ask their own skins why they testified. This ayah is the only one of the three that begins by sealing the mouth.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The account is made inescapable by locating it inside the person rather than in a document held somewhere else. That has a consequence for how deeds are understood: they are not merely observed and recorded but retained by the body that performed them. It also suggests that speech has been the instrument of evasion all along, since the mouth is the one part closed. This justice needs no prosecutor.

crossReferences.why: Names tongues, hands and feet testifying about what they used to do, in the same construction.
Extends the same idea to hearing, sight and skin, and records the accused asking their skins why they spoke.
Says hearing, sight and heart will each be questioned, placing the accounting before the Day arrives.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing your hands did this week that your mouth would describe differently. Not a scandal, just the ordinary gap: what you said about a conversation, and what you actually did inside it. Close that gap on one small item today by making the action match the account. That is this ayah brought forward into an afternoon.

studies.title: Reversed In The Making
studies.meaning: Two conditionals and then a statement. If We willed, We could blot out their eyes and leave them racing along a road they cannot see. If We willed, We could fix them where they stand so that they could go neither forward nor back. Neither is said to have happened; both are held open as capacities not exercised. Then the third ayah names something that does happen to everyone. Whoever is granted long life is reversed in his making, which the commentators read as a return of the body to weakness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the middle of the Judgement scene, and the third ayah steps out of it into present experience. No occasion is reported. Old age in a society without medicine was visible in a particular way: a man who had led caravans became someone helped to a seat. This audience had watched the reversal happen in their own fathers, which is what makes the shift from withheld power to observed fact land.

keyTerms.note: A verb for effacing something so completely that its features are gone, used of wiping out writing or a landmark. It occurs in only two ayat of the Quran, both about a power exercised or withheld.

keyTerms.gloss: We would fix them in place
keyTerms.note: A verb about transforming a thing out of its own form. The commentators read it here as being frozen where they stand, and the word occurs only once in the Quran.
To turn something upside down or send it back the way it came. Applied to a lifetime it describes strength running backwards, and the word appears in this form nowhere else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A very old man in that world returned to a condition his family recognised from infancy. He was carried, fed, watched so that he would not wander, and spoken to in a raised voice. There was no way to disguise it and no institution to take it over; the reversal happened in the room. Everyone hearing this had helped an elder in exactly the way they were once helped themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: All three verbs in this short passage are rare. One occurs in only two ayat of the Quran, the second in only one, and the verb in the third ayah for a life being turned back appears in this form nowhere else in the Book. Three unusual words in three consecutive ayat, and only the third describes something that actually happens.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage builds its case out of things withheld. Twice it names a capacity and twice declines to exercise it, which turns the ordinary functioning of a body into something granted rather than owned. Then it points at ageing, where the granting visibly stops, and asks whether that is not enough to reason from. The argument runs from a universal experience toward a conclusion the audience was refusing on other grounds entirely.

crossReferences.why: Traces the same arc directly, weakness then strength then weakness and grey hair, presented as one design.
Names the same return to a most abject age, in which a person no longer knows after having known.
States the reversal briefly and attaches it to God's knowledge and power over both ends of a life.

studies.applyIt: Spend two minutes with someone much older than you this week, on the phone if that is what you have. Do not manage the conversation. Just let the difference between what they can do now and what they once did sit in front of you without being fixed. The ayah asks you to reason from that, and reasoning starts with looking.

studies.title: We Did Not Teach Him Poetry
studies.meaning: The charge being answered is that the Prophet was a poet. The reply denies it twice, once as a fact and once as a matter of fittingness, and then names the alternative: this is a reminder and a clear recitation. The purpose clause is worth pausing on. It warns whoever is alive, which the commentators read as whoever is awake and receptive rather than merely breathing. Then the surah turns without transition to livestock, and the argument goes back to what the audience already owns.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the charge of poetry is recorded in several surahs from this period. Poets in Arabia were powerful figures, credited with knowledge from an unseen source and hired to build or destroy reputations. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Calling the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) a poet was not an aesthetic judgement. It was a way of placing the recitation into a familiar and manageable category.

keyTerms.note: From a root about perceiving or becoming aware. Poets were held to know by a route others did not have, which is why the name of their craft is built on knowing rather than on making.
A verb about something being appropriate to a person or a role. The denial is therefore doubled: he was not taught it, and it would not have suited what he was sent for.
The plain word for living. The commentators read the warning as reaching whoever is alive in the sense of awake to it, which this surah has already distinguished from those it described as sealed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe's poet was its weapon and its record. He could lift a clan's standing with one ode or wreck a rival's for a generation, and audiences at the seasonal fairs judged verse the way other societies judge law. Poetry was memorised, performed and paid for. Putting the recitation into that category would have made it something familiar, competitive, and answerable in kind.
studies.didYouKnow: The charge that the Prophet was a poet appears in several surahs, and the Quran answers it differently each time: once by listing it among a jumble of contradictory accusations, once by calling the speech that of a noble messenger and not of a poet, and once by describing what poets in that society actually did. Here the denial is made in the first person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a boundary around the recitation by naming what it is not. Poetry was the highest human speech in that world, so the denial is not that the category is too low but that it is the wrong kind. Then a purpose is supplied where a genre would go: to warn whoever is alive. That makes the text something with a function rather than a form to be admired, which is a claim about how it is to be received.

crossReferences.why: Lists the poet charge among several contradictory accusations made about the same recitation at once.
Answers the same charge by naming the speech as a noble messenger's and not a poet's at all.
Describes what poets in that society did, rambling in every style and saying what they do not do.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you receive the Quran when it is recited beautifully. There is nothing wrong with being moved by the sound. But this ayah gives the text a job, to warn whoever is alive, so read one page today in translation, slowly, as a message addressed to you, and see whether it reaches somewhere the sound alone does not.

studies.title: Made Docile For Them
studies.meaning: The animals are described entirely through what they do for people: made docile for them, some ridden and some eaten, with other uses and drinks besides. Then the question, will they not give thanks, and immediately after it the answer they actually gave. They took gods besides God, hoping to be helped. The last line closes the trap. Those gods cannot help them, and the arrangement turns out to be reversed: the worshippers stand as a garrison for their gods rather than the other way round.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Camels, sheep and goats were the material base of Arabian life, and a family's wealth was counted in head of livestock. No occasion is reported. The move from animals straight to idols is not a change of subject in this surah's argument. The same people who could itemise exactly what a camel gave them were placing their hope of rescue somewhere that gave nothing, and the contrast is the point.

keyTerms.note: From a root about lowliness and being made tractable. It names a disposition rather than a technique, so the animal's willingness to be handled is presented as something given, not achieved.
A noun formed to mean the thing that is ridden. It occurs only once in the Quran, and its form treats riding as the animal's assigned use rather than as an activity people perform.
A body of troops kept ready for a commander. Applying it to worshippers standing by their idols inverts the whole relationship, since the ones expecting rescue turn out to be on duty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel was transport, milk, meat, hide, hair for tents and dung for fire, and its docility was the basis of the entire arrangement. Anyone who had handled one knew that an animal that size complies rather than being forced. Wealth was counted in head, blood settlements were paid in camels, and a family without them could not move. This list is an inventory, not a poem.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the animal that is ridden occurs only once in the whole Quran. The final ayah of the passage then reverses an expected relationship by calling the worshippers a standing army for their gods, using the ordinary military term for troops on duty, so the people waiting to be rescued turn out to be the garrison.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage tests a claim by asking what it actually delivers. Livestock is described by its uses, item by item, and then the alternative object of hope is measured by that same standard and yields nothing. The reversal in the last line goes further still. It says the relationship is not merely useless but backwards, with the worshippers spending themselves in service of the thing they expected to be served by.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same inventory at greater length: warmth, food, beauty, carrying loads, and mounts to ride.
Names the same two uses, riding and eating, and adds the other needs that are met through them.
Calls livestock a lesson, listing drink, benefits and food, and pairs them with ships for travelling.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of what one ordinary thing gives you: a car, a phone, a job. Four or five items, specific ones. Then ask what you are actually hoping will rescue you if things go badly, and whether it would appear on any such list. The passage does the first exercise for its audience and then puts the second question without waiting for an answer.

studies.title: He Forgot His Own Making
studies.meaning: The Prophet is told not to grieve at what they say, and then the surah explains what they are. A human being does not consider that he was made from a drop, and turns into an open adversary. He strikes a comparison against God and forgets his own creation, and the argument he brings is a question: who will revive bones once they have crumbled. The commentators note that the objection carries its own answer, since the one asking it is himself the finished result of a process he never witnessed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical commentators transmit reports that a man came to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) carrying a crumbling bone, broke it in his hand and put this question, and they differ over who he was. What is not in dispute is the form of the objection. It recurs across several Meccan surahs, always as a challenge about bones or dust, and never as a question about how a first creation was managed.

keyTerms.note: A small quantity of liquid left in a vessel or at the bottom of a well. The word is deliberately unimpressive, which is the point of putting it at the head of the sentence.
One who argues a case with skill. The same construction appears in another surah in nearly identical words, pairing the drop and the arguer inside a single sentence.
Bone that has gone soft and powdery with age. The word occurs twice in the Quran, once here and once of what a destroying wind leaves behind it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bones were visible in that landscape in a way they are not now. Animals died on the routes and were left there, graves were shallow, and old burial grounds surfaced after heavy rain. A man could pick up a piece of bone on almost any journey and crumble it between his fingers. The objection was not a thought experiment. It was something a person could be holding while he said it.
studies.didYouKnow: A passage in another surah pairs exactly the same two elements in almost the same words, a human being created from a drop who then becomes an open adversary. This surah adds a third step the other does not have: he forgets his own creation. That turns the objection into an act of forgetting rather than a piece of reasoning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The failure is identified as memory rather than logic. The evidence needed to answer the question is the questioner's own existence, and that is exactly what has slipped from view. The passage also treats intellectual opposition as something that grows out of a person rather than being adopted by him, since the drop and the adversary are one subject in one sentence. And the Prophet is told first not to grieve, which frames the whole analysis as consolation.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same two facts side by side in almost identical words, the drop and the open adversary.
Runs the same argument from the drop through the stages of forming to the question of reviving the dead.
Answers the doubt about being raised by laying out the whole sequence from dust to birth to old age.

studies.applyIt: Look up how large you were at eight weeks. Not to win an argument with, just as information about yourself. The charge in this ayah is forgetting, and the repair it implies is remembering something specific about your own beginning. Two minutes of looking is enough to make concrete again the thing the passage says you have lost sight of.

studies.title: Fire From The Green Tree
studies.meaning: The answer to the question about crumbled bones comes in one clause and refuses to argue. The one who produced them the first time will revive them. Then a second sentence arrives that seems to change the subject and does not. He is the one who made fire for you out of the green tree, so that you kindle from it. The commentators identify the reference as trees whose fresh wood, rubbed together, gives flame, and read the example as fire drawn out of its own opposite.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the direct reply to the objection about decayed bone. No occasion is reported for these two ayat beyond that exchange. Making fire by friction was ordinary daily work, and the classical commentators name particular Arabian trees whose green wood was used for it. For an audience that lit its fires this way, the example was not a curiosity. It was what happened before every meal was cooked.

keyTerms.note: A verb for raising something up and developing it, used of growing a plant and of founding a settlement. It describes origination as a process rather than as an instant.
Green in the sense of fresh and full of sap, the opposite condition to dry. Naming the colour is what makes the example work, since green wood is precisely what will not burn.
The verb for starting a fire and keeping it alight. It is in the present tense and addressed directly to the audience, so the example is something they are doing rather than something reported.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fire was made by friction, a hard stick turned against a softer base until the dust caught and was fed into tinder. The classical commentators name particular trees of the region whose green branches were used for this, and the technique was known to anyone who cooked or camped. That fresh wood still wet with sap could yield a flame was not a paradox to that audience. It was simply the method.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this same example in another surah, where it asks whether the audience produced the tree of the fire they kindle or whether God did, and calls that fire a reminder. Here the example is not introduced for its own sake but as the second half of an answer about reviving crumbled bones, so fire from green wood stands in for life drawn out of what looks finished.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply works by pointing at a case the audience already accepts. Nobody in that setting doubted that fire came out of a green branch, and nobody called it impossible, though the opposition between the two states is total. Setting that beside the raising of decayed bone says the objection is about familiarity rather than possibility. And the first clause has already answered on other grounds: origination was the harder act, and it has been done.

crossReferences.why: Asks who produced the tree of the fire they kindle, and then names that fire a reminder.
States the same argument, that repeating a creation is easier for Him than beginning one.
Records the same objection about being restored and gives the same answer, the one who originated you first.

studies.applyIt: Light something today, a stove, a candle, a match, and pause for the three seconds it takes. The ayah takes the most ordinary act in a kitchen and makes it the answer to the hardest question its audience could put. Whatever you have written off as finished and beyond repair, hold it beside that for a moment before you put the match down.

studies.title: Able To Create Their Like
studies.meaning: The argument closes with a question that answers itself. Is not the one who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them. The reply then comes as a single Arabic particle, the one reserved for contradicting a negative question, so the answer is not merely yes but yes He is. And the surah names Him with an intensive form, the Creator who creates continually, joined to the name for the All-Knowing. The commentators read the difference of scale as carrying the whole force of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the last argument of the surah before its two closing ayat. The question being answered is the one about crumbled bones, widened here as far as it will go. No occasion is reported. The Meccans did not deny that God had made the heavens and the earth, and said so plainly when asked, so the passage builds on a premise this audience had already granted in other conversations.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from the root for measuring out and for capability. The same root appeared earlier in this surah for the moon being measured into stations, tying power to precision.

A particle used only to contradict a negative statement or question. Arabic keeps it separate from the ordinary word for yes, so the answer overturns the doubt rather than merely agreeing with the asker.
An intensive form of the word for creator, implying repeated and continuing making rather than one completed act. It occurs in only two ayat of the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arguments from scale were familiar in a society that measured almost everything by comparison: whose herd was larger, whose caravan longer, whose ancestors greater. A man who had built a house was not asked whether he could manage a shed. The question here runs on that ordinary logic, setting the sky and the earth against a single human body, and its audience knew exactly how such comparisons were meant to end.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensive name for the Creator used here occurs in only two ayat of the Quran, and in both it is joined to the name for the All-Knowing. The particle that answers the question is one Arabic reserves for contradicting a negative, so a single syllable does the work that English needs a whole clause to manage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument ends by changing the scale rather than by adding evidence. If the larger act is granted, the smaller one cannot be the sticking point, and the passage does not pretend this is a discovery. It is the audience's own admission turned round on them. The final name then makes creation ongoing rather than completed, which quietly removes the picture of a world made once and left to run down since.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have already done that was harder than the thing you are currently avoiding. Not a pep talk, an actual comparison: you raised a child, or you got through a year you did not think you would. The method of this ayah is to set the larger case beside the smaller one and let the hearer finish the sentence. Do that once today, honestly.

studies.title: Be And It Comes To Be
studies.meaning: The sentence answers a question raised a few ayat earlier about who could revive bones that have crumbled. It answers by removing the assumption inside the question, which was that difficulty rises with size. Command is described as speech with nothing at all between the saying and the happening. Commentators are careful about the word for command here: it does not describe a syllable God requires, but puts effective will into language a listener can follow. The second ayah turns from mechanism to praise.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and these are the closing lines of the surah. The ayat before them report someone crumbling an old bone and asking who could bring it back. The answer works backwards through the first origination, then fire drawn out of green wood, then the making of the heavens, and arrives here. The commentators report an occasion involving a Meccan objector with a decayed bone, though their accounts name different men.

keyTerms.note: One word covering an order given and a matter being handled. The Quran uses it for both, so the sentence describes a decision and its execution without a gap between them.
The shortest possible imperative in Arabic, two letters. Its brevity is part of the argument, since the whole distance between intention and existence is expressed in the smallest available word.
An intensive form of the ordinary word for kingdom, occurring only four times in the Quran. It names sovereignty as a realm rather than as an authority exercised over one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A chief's word was the machinery of that world. An order spoken in the assembly moved men, animals and goods, and its force was measured precisely by how little distance lay between the saying and the doing. A man whose instructions needed repeating or enforcing was known to be weak. Everyone listening could rank authority on that scale, so a word requiring nothing after it described the top of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for dominion in the final ayah is an intensified form of the ordinary word for a kingdom, and it appears only four times in the entire Quran. Once it is what Abraham was shown of the heavens and the earth, twice it is put to those who reject the message as a question, and once it closes this surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Power and effort are separated completely. Creation is described without any process at all, which is a claim about what kind of thing God is rather than about how quickly an event happens. Then the surah declines to leave the argument standing as a proof. It closes with glorification and with a direction of travel instead, so the demonstration ends by turning the reader rather than by settling a dispute.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you have privately filed as impossible: a person who will not change, a situation with no exit. You do not have to talk yourself out of the judgement. Just identify the assumption you are leaning on, which is usually that size and difficulty run together. This ayah takes that assumption apart and offers nothing else.
